title: Sita won't stay behind
hookLine: Rama asks Sita to wait at home, and she claims her share of his road
carry: a partner in dharma shares the road
tomorrow: Rama has a list of dangers. will it stop her?

cards: Rama comes home with his news, and with a plan for Sita. She'll stay in Ayodhya and wait for him. He has thought it through, kindly, carefully, and alone.
In Valmiki's telling, Sita is many things in this scene, and quiet isn't the first of them. She hears the whole plan out. Then, piece by piece, she takes it apart.

teach.b: Sita has been waiting at home for the procession. She sees Rama come in alone and pale, with no royal umbrella and no music, and she knows something's wrong. He tells her everything, then gives instructions.
Stay here. Serve my father and my mothers. Don't praise me in front of Bharata.
Keep your vows, live simply, and wait for me. Valmiki says Sita answers out of love and anger together. Father, mother, brother, son: each lives out their own fortune.
But a wife shares her husband's.

teach.h: IF YOU'RE SENT TO THE FOREST, SO AM I.
teach.b: If you've been sent to the forest, so have I. If you go today, I'll walk ahead of you, trampling the thorns and sharp grass so your path is easier.
And she'd rather be in the forest with him, seeing the mountains and the lotus ponds, than in a palace without him. Rama decided for both of them, kindly and alone. Sita refuses to be decided for.
Here's the teaching under her argument.
You met the word at her wedding: a Hindu wife is a sahadharmachari, a companion on the path of dharma.

At a Hindu wedding the couple takes seven steps together beside the sacred fire, and by the old words, at the seventh step they become friends. Sita is holding Rama to that. His duty is hers to share, thorns included.
And that's still the promise when a couple takes those seven steps today: one road, walked together, even when it turns hard.

how: At a Hindu wedding the couple takes seven steps together beside the sacred fire (saptapadi) and become partners in dharma; Sita's argument can be read as what that promise means when the road turns hard.

games.q: a cousin at a Hindu wedding asks what the seven steps by the fire actually promise. by Sita's argument, what fits?
o: one road, shared: each one's dharma becomes the other's to walk too.
the bride agrees to follow whatever the groom decides.
good luck for the first seven years.
games.why: Sita wouldn't be decided for. as a partner in dharma, she claimed her share of Rama's road, thorns included.

practice: At a Hindu wedding the couple takes seven steps by the fire. Take seven slow breaths as seven steps. With each one, picture someone whose road you share: a partner, a parent, a friend.
If you pray, offer each step to God for them; if you don't, simply wish them well. On the seventh, hold them as Sita held Rama: a friend whose road is yours too.

wordCard.voice: Sita's argument. Asked to stay behind, she answers with love and anger: a wife shares her husband's fortune, and if he's sent to the forest, so is she.

orig.note: Sanskrit sītā: a furrow. her name recalls how Janaka found her in a plowed field.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: a partner in dharma shares the road. Rama has one more try in him. Day five hundred twenty-six.
